metadata.title: Content Strategy for Affiliate Marketing Sites [3.3]
metadata.author: Ahrefs
metadata.shortDescription:
In this lesson, you'll learn the content strategy you should use to create a successful affiliate marketing website. 

***************************************
Additional Affiliate Marketing Resources

Affiliate Marketing Course [playlist] ► https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLvJ_dXFSpd2vBOn-szyf73Z3Ll3tCBTRc

Keyword Research for Affiliate Marketing Sites [3.2] ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MmhN3laA2_g

Affiliate Marketing Tutorials [playlist] ► https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLvJ_dXFSpd2sOqo2q7SzTCizxrMFxZFle

Content Marketing For Beginners: Complete Guide ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0R_3iarc8IA

Content Hubs: Where SEO and Content Marketing Meet ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nIbJI1kCxrU

***************************************
The content marketing strategy we'll be using revolves around organizing the list of topics from your keyword research list into logical structures that'll help grow your SEO traffic to your affiliate site.

You'll learn how to create a massive hub of related content covering all your niche's essential topics. And more importantly, you’ll learn how all of this is related to creating "topical authority" for your site.

Topical authority is typically looked at as including two things:

► topical coverage (content);
► backlinks

Watch the video to learn more about building so-called ‘topical authority’ for your affiliate site.

Before you start building your web of related content, you'll have to map topics together. And the most efficient way to map affiliate topics is by creating product clusters.

A product cluster is a simple content structure that connects a general comparison post with multiple product review posts.

#affiliatemarketing #affiliatemarketingcourse #contentstrategy

Be sure to subscribe for more actionable marketing and SEO tutorials.
https://www.youtube.com/AhrefsCom?sub_confirmation=1

STAY TUNED:
Ahrefs ► https://ahrefs.com/
YouTube ► https://www.youtube.com/AhrefsCom?sub_confirmation=1
Facebook ► https://www.facebook.com/Ahrefs
Twitter ►https://twitter.com/ahrefs

segments.text: Hey, it's Sam Oh and in this lesson, I'm going to walk you through a simple affiliate marketing
content strategy.
More specifically, we'll be taking the list of topics from your keyword research and
organizing them into logical structures that'll help grow your SEO traffic to your
affiliate site.
Now, as I mentioned in lesson 3.1., we want to create a massive web of related content,
covering all of the important topics in our niche.
And the main benefit here is that all of these relevant pages will be connected
and essentially work together to build what SEOs loosely call "topical authority."
And if we had to define topical authority, it's when a website becomes an authoritative
source on a given topic in the eyes of visitors and search engines.
Now, the two parts that make up so-called "topical authority" are topical coverage,
meaning content, and backlinks.
We'll talk about the latter a bit later because I want to illustrate
the importance of topical coverage.
Let's say you have a site in the golf niche.
If you publish a post on the best golf clubs, no one's going to think:
"Oh yeah…they're the authority" in golf or golf clubs or golf equipment.
To become the go to place for information on golf, you'd need to cover topics like "best
golf balls," "best putters," "best golf shoes," "how to hit a driver 300 yards," "what is a handicap in
golf," and I could go on for hours.
Plus, the content would actually need to be good.
Now, even this example hardly illustrates becoming an authority in the golf niche
because there's just so many things you'd need to cover because golf is a huge topic.
This is why focusing on a sub-niche is a much better approach to building
topical authority.
And this is the way we chose a niche in module 2.
So you'd cover topics like: "best golf balls," "pro v1 golf ball review,"
"pro v1x golf ball review," "taylormade tp5 review," "how many dimples are on
a golf ball," "how to properly clean golf balls," "which golf ball generates the most spin,"
"best golf balls for high handicappers," and add another hundred or so topics.
Assuming your content is of high quality, over time, people will begin to see you as
an expert in your niche and because of that, they'll more likely link to your web pages
because it's well-trusted.
Again, I'm barely scratching the surface, but my point should be clear: building so-called topical
authority a) requires extensive topical coverage; b) is much more achievable
in a sub niche because of a); and c) building it is a win-win for visitors and website owners.
For visitors, they'll find a plethora of resources to dig through on your site.
And for website owners, you'll likely have better potential to rank for topically related keywords,
assuming your content gets linked to.
And I'll expand on why topical authority may help your rankings later in this lesson.
Now, if you've been building your site with me throughout this course, then
you should have narrowed in on a sub-niche and done all your
keyword research for that sub-niche.
I chose baby products as my main niche and car seats as my sub-niche.
And in total, I generated a list of 239 car-seat related keywords that I also categorized into
the four different "types" of affiliate keywords.
General comparisons; Branded comparisons; Product reviews; and T&A keywords.
The only major thing that's left to do in this planning stage is to map related
topics together so we can start building our web of related content.
And we'll be using our keyword lists to do this.
Now, if you get no clue what I'm talking about, then I highly recommend going
back to lesson 3.2. where I walked you through how to do keyword research for
affiliate marketing sites.
But if you're all caught up, then let's talk about perhaps the most efficient
way to map affiliate topics.
And that's by creating product clusters.
A product cluster is a simple content structure that connects a general comparison post
with multiple product review posts.
Let's look at what this might look like for my car seat site.
So first, I'll choose a general comparison topic from my list like "best car seat for
3-year olds."
This topic will sit at the top of our pyramid.
Now, because general comparison topics will require product comparisons and
recommendations, we'll need to choose some car seats to compare in our post.
And in my opinion, the best place to start is to draw from real-life experiences.
For example, I actually own nine car seats – so it's fair to say that I've done my share of
research and real-life testing.
Now, I also have a couple kids that are now older than three and so I know that
the types of car seats we'll be covering are "convertible car seats."
One of our car seats is the Diono Radian 3RXT which I really like so I'll definitely include
it in my round-up.
Now, visually speaking, we would just add a branch under our main topic:
"best car seat for 3-year olds" and call it "Diono Radian 3RXT review."
Now, another car seat we have is the Britax Marathon which I also like and
would recommend.
So let's add another branch.
Now, I'm not particularly happy with some of the other convertible car seats I've bought,
so let's look at our product review keywords to see which other car seats we could potentially add.
Now, I've already gone ahead and looked at product specs, reviews,
and installation videos for 14 different convertible car seats.
And after researching, I've narrowed down our list of "best car seats for
3-year olds" to a total of six car seats.
The two that I have hands-on experience with, the Britax one4life, Graco Extend2fit,
Graco 4ever dlx, and the Safety 1st Go and Grow.
So let's add branches to our flow chart for each of these models.
So to review, we know we're going to create a post on the best car seats for 3-year olds
plus, we're going to write six different product reviews for each model in our
general comparison post like "Britax one4life review", "Graco extend2fit review" and so on.
Now, from an on-page perspective, we can simply "connect" these pages by using an internal link
from our general comparison post to our product reviews.
And it would also make sense to link from our product reviews to our general comparison post.
We now have a product cluster.
Now, the reason why I call product clusters efficient is because as your library of product
reviews gets bigger, creating content for general comparisons gets faster and easier.
For example, when we go to create a post on let's say… "the best convertible car seats for
small cars," we've already covered the Diono Radian 3RXT review in our best car seat for
3-year olds post.
And that model just happens to be the go-to car seat for small cars.
Now, branded comparisons also fit seamlessly into product clusters.
Looking at our list of branded comparison keywords, you'll see that there's this topic
"graco extend2fit vs 4ever".
Well, we just wrote two product reviews for these so writing a branded comparison
post would be super-easy.
And of course, we could easily add internal links to the product reviews
whether they're one-way or reciprocal in a very organic way.
Alright, the last type of keywords on our list are T&A keywords which again
stands for trust and authority.
And these are mostly informational topics.
Now, these topics may not directly impact your revenue but they serve
important purposes: they can help you earn more backlinks, reach larger audiences,
and build trust and authority.
Now, unlike product clusters, informational posts on affiliate sites typically have less of
a pyramid-type structure to them.
For example, if you have four pages on T&A topics, they won't necessarily link
together creating a perfect pyramid.
Internal linking on these pages will mostly come down to "do it if and when it makes sense."
For example, let's say we're a writing post on car seat safety.
It would be perfectly natural to link to another page on "when car seats expire",
"when you should turn the car seat around from rear to forward facing"
and "requirements to change to a booster seat."
These are all related to car seat safety and they all happen to be
topics on our T&A keyword list.
Now, it would also make perfect sense to link from our post on "when do car seats expire"
to our commercial page on "best car seats" because people reading that post may need
to buy a new one and could probably use some help narrowing their search
to an appropriate product.
As you can see, creating these structures and mapping content isn't so much about
strict adherence as it is about creating a strong foundation for your content SEO.
When you have a big list of topics and you prioritize based on search volumes or keyword
difficulty scores, it's tough to visualize the relationships between your content.
And what happens more often than not, is that you haphazardly do internal linking
creating poor structure, which just makes ranking your pages harder than it has to be.
But by having a solid internal linking plan, you're going to do yourself a couple favors
that should ultimately help you rank higher in Google and get more free traffic to your pages.
#1. You'll create a better user experience for your visitors by providing them with relevant
resources that may be helpful to them.
And #2. You'll facilitate the flow of PageRank which will help your pages
rank higher in Google.
And without getting too technical, that just means that when one of your pages gets
backlinks, the pages that it links to will also benefit from that backlink –
although to a lesser degree.
Alright, so now that we've mapped out our content, we'll need to actually build out our site.
And I won't go into how to create a WordPress blog or suggest specific themes because a lot
of that is entirely up to your preferences.
But I do want to talk about two super- important things related to site creation.
And these are your homepage's content and your website's navigation menu.
And that's coming up in the next lesson.
I'll see you there.

Well, we just wrote two product reviews for these so writing a branded comparison post would be super-easy. And of course, we could easily add internal links to the product reviews whether they're one-way or reciprocal in a very organic way. Alright, the last type of keywords on our list are T&A keywords which again stands for trust and authority. And these are mostly informational topics. Now, these topics may not directly impact your revenue but they serve important purposes: they can help you earn more backlinks, reach larger audiences, and build trust and authority. Now, unlike product clusters, informational posts on affiliate sites typically have less of a pyramid-type structure to them. For example, if you have four pages on T&A topics, they won't necessarily link together creating a perfect pyramid. Internal linking on these pages will mostly come down to "do it if and when it makes sense." For example, let's say we're a writing post on car seat safety. It would be perfectly natural to link to another page on "when car seats expire", "when you should turn the car seat around from rear to forward facing" and "requirements to change to a booster seat." These are all related to car seat safety and they all happen to be topics on our T&A keyword list. Now, it would also make perfect sense to link from our post on "when do car seats expire" to our commercial page on "best car seats" because people reading that post may need to buy a new one and could probably use some help narrowing their search to an appropriate product. As you can see, creating these structures and mapping content isn't so much about strict adherence as it is about creating a strong foundation for your content SEO. When you have a big list of topics and you prioritize based on search volumes or keyword difficulty scores, it's tough to visualize the relationships between your content. And what happens more often than not, is that you haphazardly do internal linking creating poor structure, which just makes ranking your pages harder than it has to be. But by having a solid internal linking plan, you're going to do yourself a couple favors that should ultimately help you rank higher in Google and get more free traffic to your pages. #1. You'll create a better user experience for your visitors by providing them with relevant resources that may be helpful to them. And #2. You'll facilitate the flow of PageRank which will help your pages rank higher in Google. And without getting too technical, that just means that when one of your pages gets backlinks, the pages that it links to will also benefit from that backlink – although to a lesser degree. Alright, so now that we've mapped out our content, we'll need to actually build out our site. And I won't go into how to create a WordPress blog or suggest specific themes because a lot of that is entirely up to your preferences. But I do want to talk about two super- important things related to site creation. And these are your homepage's content and your website's navigation menu. And that's coming up in the next lesson. I'll see you there.

metadata.title: SaaS Competitor Comparison Pages: Why you NEED to Build them
metadata.author: Rock The Rankings: B2B SaaS GEO & SEO Agency
metadata.shortDescription:
Competitor comparison landing pages are a classic SaaS strategy to drive bottom-of-the-funnel traffic and conversions when prospects are in the transactional intent phase of the marketing funnel.

These pages are crucial for helping your customers to understand whether they’re really the right fit for your service, or not – and are an extremely effective way to hone in on your ideal customer, rather than simply adding customers that will eventually churn.

Many SaaS organizations either:

- Neglect creating these pages all together as they find it unethical to say anything that could shed the competition in a negative light
Create these pages, but haven’t really gone about it in the best way possible (i.e. it’s all about “us, us, us.” or beating up the competition)

-Competitor comparison landing pages have become almost essential at this point in order to not allow your competitors to control the conversation on how their product stacks up against yours.

These pages can also be extremely effective for young SaaS startups with little brand recognition, and minimal search traffic.

Use our best practice guide and template to get started: https://www.rocktherankings.com/competitor-comparison-landing-pages/

segments.text: Hey paper callers, I'm Jordan Soto with
Ringba, the premier call tracking
platform for paper call marketers. In
this episode, we're going to explain why
paper call affiliates need their own
call tracking.
Affiliate marketers in the paper call
space are typically at a disadvantage
when they rely on their partners
tracking platform for their payouts and
statistics. This problem can cost
affiliates substantial lost revenue from
unmonetized calls, while also leading to
overspending on media buying from a lack
of visibility into key metrics that are
driving their calls and conversions.
This lack of information also impedes on
affiliates' ability to negotiate with
their partners. They often back
themselves into a corner negotiating
from a point of weakness because they
don't have multiple buyers that can
compete for their calls. And even if
they did have multiple buyers, without
call tracking technology, affiliates
will never be able to properly load
balance and route their calls.
Let's back up a second. As you probably
know, affiliate marketers are
third-parties that provide calls to
brokers, paper call networks, call
centers, and other businesses that are
looking for high-intent leads to sell
their products and services. They're
typically compensated for every phone
call they generate. That's why it's
called pay-per-call.
In other words, the affiliate is paid
only when a call is connected to a buyer
that meets all of the predetermined
payout criteria. Here are some examples
of payout criteria: minimum call
duration, area code or geographic
location, hours of operation, specific
demographic information such as age or
income, and more.
When an affiliate generates a call that
meets all of the requirements set for
the campaign, it's considered a a
call and they are paid. Most of the
time, when dealing with pay per call
networks, affiliates are paid a flat
rate per call, and they're sometimes
given bonuses based on volume or
quality. More sophisticated affiliates
use real-time bidding software,
like Ringba, to get buyers to bid on
their calls, making sure they get paid
top dollar every time.
No control over call flow. Affiliates
that don't use their own call tracking
software give control over their destiny
to pay per call networks or their other
call buyers. There are all kinds of
games that call buyers can play that
allow them to take full advantage of
affiliates. For example, the buyer may
have a concurrency cap that is shared
among multiple affiliates that may not
allocate any specific affiliate
guaranteed capacity. This will cause
dropped calls to not be paid for and
make it almost impossible to buy paid
media. The worst part is that in most
circumstances, buyers won't even
disclose if this happens. Alternatively,
buyers may quickly ask the caller for
their phone number and say that they'll
call them right back before the call's
payout duration has been met. This is
known as callback fraud, and if you
don't have your own call tracking with
recordings in place, you'll never be
able to catch it.
No transparency.
Affiliates will also not be aware if a
buyer decides to bounce calls, misreport
the number of raw calls, or misreport
the number of calls that met the
conversion qualifications without their
own tracking. Perhaps the partner
involved is honest, but calls that go
over the buyer's capping restriction are
simply abandoned. While this situation
remains honest, the affiliate is once
again at a disadvantage because the
advertising dollars spent to generate
the overflow calls are lost.
Unfortunately, due to the human
requirement to answer the phone and
unpredictable nature of call flow, this
happens a lot. Call tracking can solve
all of these problems.
No ability to scale with multiple
buyers. Affiliates should have multiple
buyers for the same campaigns at all
times. Otherwise, they're in a single
point situation of failure where if
their buyer has a technical issue, has
no capacity, decides to cut the
affiliate off for various reasons, or
other instances where their campaign has
to be paused,
the affiliate does not have anywhere to
send their calls. And this can be
dangerous for the affiliates who don't
plan ahead. Due to the potential for
easy money, affiliates are generally not
thinking for the long term, and this
lack of foresight creates a dangerous
blind spot for their business.
Affiliates should seek to find multiple
buyers for their campaign. Typically,
the more calls, the more buyers they
should find, but in almost all
circumstances, a minimum of three buyers
is suggested. This gives the affiliate
the ability to negotiate between
multiple buyers, see which is actually
performing better, and protect
themselves from potential downtime. By
having more buyers, the affiliate is now
in the power position for negotiating
payouts, and can pull their traffic from
their partners at any time without
risking their business. Call tracking
software makes this all possible.
So, what's the solution?
Ringba, of course. Rule number one for
all types of online advertising for
affiliates and marketers of any kind is
track everything. Many affiliates we've
encountered in the call space are
reluctant to track their activities
because, unlike clicks, which have a
very low tracking cost, call tracking is
significantly more expensive. Yes, it is
possible to run campaigns without your
own call tracking. Many affiliates do,
but we have yet to encounter someone not
tracking their calls that didn't have a
significant amount of lost calls and
wasted advertising spend. And that is a
big problem. The solution for affiliates
is to leverage call tracking like Ringba
to reduce their advertising spend, keep
their partners honest with independent
verifiable statistics, and to sell off
overflow wherever possible. The best
part is that almost 100% of the time,
call tracking actually turns into a
profit center for affiliates. For
affiliates, using your own call tracking
puts you in the driver's seat, giving
you control over your call flow and the
ability to take paper call affiliate
business to the next level. This video

Imagine a business model where you don't need a warehouse, you don't need inventory, and you don't even need your own product. 📉📈

It’s called Lead Arbitrage (or Pay Per Lead), and it is essentially the digital equivalent of day trading. You buy attention from platforms like Facebook for $10, generate a lead, and sell that lead to a business for $20. You profit the difference.

In this video, I break down exactly how this high-leverage model works, how companies like "Lower My Bills" used it to exit for over $300 Million, and why I am personally moving my marketing agency from a standard retainer model to this performance-based approach.

If you are a media buyer, agency owner, or entrepreneur looking for a scalable business model, you need to understand the mechanics of being the "Hunter" (Publisher) and finding the "Chef" (Buyer).

In this video, you’ll learn: 
✅ The exact math behind Lead Arbitrage (Cost per Lead vs. Sale Price). 
✅ The "Hunter vs. Chef" analogy for understanding the market. 
✅ Case Study: How "Lower My Bills" sold for $380M with ugly ads. 
✅ Key definitions: Affiliates, Publishers, Networks, and Aggregators. 
✅ Why big brands like NerdWallet and LendingTree are actually arbitrage companies.

metadata.title: How To Generate Tracking Links | Everflow Mini Webinars
metadata.author: Everflow - Partner Marketing Platform
metadata.shortDescription:
Master the fundamental skill of generating tracking links in Everflow with this complete and easy-to-follow guide. We'll show you three different methods for creating partner and offer-specific links, from using the quick Tracking Link Generator to performing bulk actions on the offer and partner pages.

Learn how to add sub IDs, generate QR codes, create impression trackers, and utilize advanced features to build the perfect tracking link for any campaign.

## In this tutorial, you will learn 3 methods:

* **Method 1: The Tracking Link Generator**: Use the quick-access global tool in the left-hand menu to instantly create a single tracking link by selecting any offer and partner.
* **Method 2: From the Offer Page**: Generate links for a specific offer with advanced options, including creating impression trackers, advertiser test links, and bulk-generating links or QR codes for *all* approved partners at once.
* **Method 3: From the Partner Page**: Easily grab tracking links for a specific partner across one or multiple offers they are approved for, streamlining your workflow.

### We will also cover:

* **Advanced Customization**: How to add Additional Parameters (like `sub1`-`sub5` and `source_id`) to your links for granular, in-depth tracking.
* **Link Types & Outputs**: Understand the difference between standard Redirect Links, Direct Linking, and Impression Trackers.
* **Exporting Links**: See how to quickly copy your link, generate a QR code, or share it with full offer details.

This tutorial is essential for any affiliate manager, media buyer, or partner who needs to generate and customize tracking links within the Everflow platform.

🔗 **For more in-depth articles and guides, visit the Everflow Helpdesk:**
[https://helpdesk.everflow.io/]

🚀 **New to Everflow? Discover the ultimate platform for managing your partnerships:**
[https://www.everflow.io/]

Don't forget to like this video and subscribe to our channel for more helpful tutorials!

#Everflow #TrackingLink #AffiliateMarketing #PartnerMarketing #LinkGenerator #PerformanceMarketing #AdTech #SaaS #DigitalMarketing

metadata.title: Connect Everflow to Your CRM: Pay on Quality, Not Just Quantity | Everflow Mini Webinars
metadata.author: Everflow - Partner Marketing Platform
metadata.shortDescription:
Everflow is a performance marketing platform that helps businesses track and optimize their affiliate programs. This video features Everflow expert Isaac Maier discussing the benefits of connecting Everflow to your CRM. By integrating Everflow with your CRM, you can:

Pay on Quality, Not Just Quantity: Gain visibility into the entire customer lifecycle and reward affiliates based on high-quality outcomes rather than just lead volume.

Reduce Waste and Fraud: Automatically filter out poor quality leads, such as disconnected numbers or duplicates, before payouts are triggered.

Speed Up Your Sales Cycle: Transition from days-long manual data uploads to near-instantaneous syncs, allowing your sales team to strike while the lead is hot.

Optimize Your Partner Network: Identify which affiliates are sending long-term loyal customers and adjust incentives to drive more high-value traffic.

Video Timestamps

0:04 - 0:53: The Problem: Paying for "Junk Leads" vs. Outcomes

0:54 - 1:18: Battle #1: Speed to Lead - The 5-Minute Window

1:19 - 1:42: Battle #2: The Manual Reconciliation Nightmare

1:43 - 1:59: Solution #1: Zapier (Small-to-Midsize Businesses)

2:00 - 2:12: Solution #2: Webhooks (Custom and Proprietary CRMs)

2:13 - 2:28: Solution #3: Direct API (Enterprise, Finance, and Legal)

2:29 - 2:50: Rewarding the Full Lifecycle: Lead, Retainer, and Settlement

2:51 - 3:23: Advanced Reporting with Snowflake, Domo, and Firehose

3:24 - 3:42: Outro: Stop Paying for Raw Volume

Searchable Keywords & Meta Data
Keywords: Everflow CRM Integration, Performance Marketing, Affiliate Tracking Software, Sales Pipeline Optimization, CRM Feedback Loops, Pay Per Lead Quality, Marketing Automation, Salesforce Integration, HubSpot Integration, Zapier for Marketing.

Take a look here: https://www.everflow.io/?affid=64316

metadata.title: What The FTC Actually Requires You To Disclose As An Affiliate
metadata.author: Hustle Audit
metadata.shortDescription: Today we'll look into the real FTC Endorsement Guides, what influencers and affiliates are legally required to disclose, not the watered-down version repeated online. Using the FTC's July 2023 updated Endorsement Guides, the 'clear and conspicuous' standard, the official Disclosures 101 guidance, the October 2021 Notice of Penalty Offenses sent to 700+ companies, the per-violation civil penalty (raised to roughly $53,000), and the 2020 Teami case ($15.2M judgment, warning letters to Cardi B and Jordin Sparks), we map exactly what counts as a 'material connection,' why #ad buried in hashtags fails, and the single test that tells you whether your disclosure is actually legal.

segments.text: Almost everyone selling something online
thinks they understand the rules. Tag it
#ad, drop it somewhere in the post, and
you're covered. That belief is wrong in
ways that have already cost real people
real money. The Federal Trade
Commission's endorsement guides do not
ask whether you typed the word ad. They
ask whether an ordinary person would
actually notice it. So, we pulled the
real rules apart, line by line, and
tested the gap between what people think
the law says and what it actually
requires. First, define what's actually
being regulated because most people get
this wrong at the start.
The rule is not about the word
advertisement. It is about something the
commission calls a material connection.
A material connection exists anytime
there is a relationship between you and
the brand that your audience would not
reasonably expect, and that could affect
how much weight they give your
recommendation.
That is broad on purpose. It covers
being paid in cash. It covers free or
discounted products. It covers an
affiliate link that pays you a
commission when someone buys. It covers
employment, a family tie, even a close
personal friendship with the founder.
If any of those exist and your audience
can't see them, the law says you have to
tell them.
The trigger is not money changing hands
in a particular way.
The trigger is a connection the viewer
wouldn't guess on their own. Now, the
part that does the real work, and the
part almost everyone fails. A disclosure
isn't legal just because it exists
somewhere. It has to be, in the
commission's exact words, clear and
conspicuous. The official test is plain.
The disclosure must be difficult to miss
and easily understood by an ordinary
member of your audience. That single
standard quietly kills most of what
passes for disclosure online.
#ad sitting at the end of 15 other
hashtags doesn't count because no one
reads to the bottom of a hashtag pile.
A disclosure hidden behind a more
button, where the viewer has to tap to
expand the caption, doesn't count
because most people never tap.
Tiny gray text on a busy background
doesn't count. And vague little tags
like CP or spawn or collab or just the
word thanks don't count either because
an ordinary person doesn't reliably
decode them as paid advertising. The
commission's own guidance is blunt about
this. Don't bury it. Put it where the
audience actually looks before they
engage with the recommendation. These
aren't dusty old rules either.
The commission formally updated its
endorsement guides in July of 2023, the
biggest revision in over a decade, and
the changes tighten the screws
specifically for the way people sell
things now.
Three pieces matter most. First, the
updated guides made clear that a
platform's own built-in disclosure tool
is not enough on its own. The little
paid partnership label some apps add
does not automatically satisfy the law.
You still owe your own clear disclosure
on top of it. Second, the definition of
an endorsement was widened to explicitly
capture fake reviews, paid for star
ratings, and even tags of a brand in a
photo. A tag can be an endorsement.
Third, the guides put new weight on the
brands themselves, signaling they should
be monitoring the people they pay rather
than looking away.
The headline from the 2023 update is
simple, more of what creators do every
day now counts as an endorsement and
fewer of the shortcuts count as a
disclosure. So, what happens if you
ignore all this? Here the numbers stop
being abstract. In October of 2021, the
commission sent a notice of penalty
offenses to more than 700 large
companies, a legal maneuver that does
one specific thing, it puts those firms
on formal notice that deceptive
endorsement practices can now trigger
civil penalties in federal court.
At the time the cap sat near $43,000 per
violation. That ceiling is tied to
inflation and by 2025 it had climbed to
roughly $53,000 per violation.
Read the phrase carefully, per
violation.
The commission's position is that each
non-compliant post, each missing
disclosure, each undisclosed affiliate
link can count as its own separate
violation.
A single campaign of 10 posts is not one
exposure.
It is potentially 10.
The math is deliberately frightening,
and it is meant to be. And this is not
theoretical, because the commission has
already pulled the trigger.
The clearest example is the Teami case.
Teami sold detox teas with health claims
it couldn't back up, promoted by paid
celebrity influencers whose posts buried
the paid relationship out of sight.
In March of 2020, the commission
settled. The judgment was $15.2 million,
partially suspended down to a $1 million
payment reflected what the company could
actually pay.
But the detail that should matter to
every creator is what the commission did
next.
It sent warning letters directly to 10
of the influencers, including Cardi B
and Jordan Sparks, telling them their
disclosures were not good enough.
The specific instruction in those
letters reads like a checklist for
everyone else. The disclosure of a
material connection must sit above the
more button, where it is visible without
expanding the caption, and it must not
be buried inside a clump of hashtags.
The brand paid the millions. The
influencers got named. Both ends of the
deal were on the hook. Step back, and
the ways disclosures actually fail
collapse into a short repeating list,
and almost none of them involve
forgetting to disclose entirely.
The failures are people who think they
disclosed.
Failure one,
placement.
The disclosure existed, but it sat below
the fold, after the more button, or at
the bottom of a video the viewer
scrolled past.
Failure two,
camouflage. It was technically there,
lost inside a wall of hashtags, or
styled in low-contrast text that the eye
slides over.
Failure three, vagueness.
They used a code word, SP or collab, or
a vague thank you that an ordinary
person can't reliably read as
advertising.
Failure four,
format mismatch. They put the disclosure
in the written caption of a video that
most people watch on mute and never
read.
So, a spoken or on-screen disclosure was
actually required.
And failure five, outsourcing to the
platform, assuming the app's little
built-in label did the whole job by
itself.
Notice the through line.
In every single case, the person
believed they were compliant.
The standard isn't intent. It's whether
an ordinary viewer would have noticed.
So, strip it all down. The FTC
endorsement guides are not a vibe and
not a hashtag.
They rest on two questions you can run
against anything you post in 10 seconds.
Question one,
is there a material connection your
audience wouldn't already expect?
A payment, a free product, an affiliate
commission, a relationship of any kind.
If yes, you owe a disclosure.
Question two, would an ordinary member
of your audience actually notice and
understand that disclosure?
Without tapping more, without decoding
slang,
without reading to the end of a hashtag
pile, in the same format they're
consuming the content. If the honest
answer to that second question is no,
then in the eyes of the law, you have
not disclosed at all, no matter how many
times the letters A and D appear in your
caption.
That is the whole test.
Material connection, clearly and
conspicuously disclosed, where the
viewer will genuinely see it. Everything
else, the warning letters, the proposed
penalties, the seven-figure judgments,
is just the price of failing those two
questions.
Audit closed.

metadata.author: eternalsoulwriter
metadata.shortDescription:
Do you really need an affiliate disclosure? Is #ad enough? 
Where should you disclose Amazon affiliate links on YouTube, your website, Pinterest, Instagram, TikTok, or your blog?

In this video, I break down what the official Amazon Associates Program policies and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) guidance say about affiliate disclosures. I'll explain when disclosures are required, where they should appear, and share the disclosure workflow I personally use across my content as an Amazon Influencer.

In this video, I cover:
• What an affiliate disclosure is
• Why Amazon affiliate disclosures matter
• Amazon Associates disclosure requirements
• FTC disclosure guidelines for influencers
• Where to place affiliate disclosures
• Affiliate disclosures for YouTube videos
• Website and blog disclosure best practices
• Social media disclosure requirements
• Is #ad enough?
• Amazon's required Associate statement
• Common affiliate disclosure mistakes
• My personal disclosure workflow
• How I stay transparent across multiple platforms
• Best practices for Amazon Influencers and Amazon Associates

📚 Official resources mentioned in this video:

FTC – Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers:
https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers

Amazon Associates – Appropriate Conduct:
https://affiliate-program.amazon.com/help/node/topic/GHQNZAU6669EZS98

This video reflects Amazon's and the FTC's guidance as of July 2026. Always check the latest official documentation, as policies can change.

Join my private Facebook group for Amazon Influencers:
https://www.facebook.com/groups/eternasoulwriter

Explore my world:
https://linktr.ee/artwithcarmen

Disclosure: Some of the links above may be affiliate links, which means I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you.

As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.

segments.text: Have you ever wondered, do you really need an affiliate disclosure? Is the #ad enough? Do
you need a disclaimer on your website? Should you add one on your YouTube videos, on Pinterest pins,
Instagram post, maybe your blog? If you have searched online, you have probably
found completely different answers depending on who you ask. So instead of relying on opinions,
I decided to read the official documentation from Amazon and the Federal Trade Commissions,
also known as FTC . So in this video, I will show you exactly what they say, what you actually need
to disclose, okay? Where disclosure should go and how I personally stay compliant across my content.
And don't worry, I'm not a lawyer, so this isn't a legal advice. Okay, great. I'm simply sharing
what the official guidance says so you can make informed decisions for your own business. Hi,
my name is Carmen. Welcome to my YouTube channel. I'm happy to have you here. So, let's get started.
What is an affiliate disclosure? First, let's clear up what an affiliate disclosure actually
is. Okay, great. Pay attention. An affiliate disclosure is simple. A statement that tells
your audience you may earn commissions if they purchase something through your affiliate links.
It doesn't cost them anything extra. It doesn't change the price they pay. It simply lets people
know that you have a financial relationship with the company you're recommending. Simple. That
transparency is actually what both Amazon and the FTC wants. Now why are disclosure this important?
There are really 3 reasons , reason number 1 is : they are required by Amazon. Okay. If you are
participating in the Amazon associate program or the Amazon influencer program simple. The 2nd
reason : the FTC requires influencers and content creators to disclose material relationships with
brands whenever those relationship could influence recommendations. And the 3rd reason : being you
know transparent actually builds trust. Okay. Personally, I would much rather tell
people upfront than have someone wonder later whether I was earning a commission. Okay. Now,
what Amazon requires? Let's start with Amazon own policy. According to Amazon associate program
requirements whenever you share an affiliate link you should include a clear and conspicuous okay
disclosure near those links. Amazon even gives example like #ad , #CommissionsEarned or paid
link. These are considered acceptable link level disclosure. Amazon also requires associate to
identify themselves using this exact statement. Write it down. Okay. " As an Amazon associate,
I earn from qualifying purchases. " Notice something important. Amazon specifically
provides that wording. Personally, I don't change it. Okay? I use it exactly as written.
Now where this you know statement should go for websites , for blogs , right you can include
that statement on your website where it's clearly visible obviously , so many creators also place it

metadata.shortDescription:
Presented by 'The fyi by Find Your Influence' Content Series 

In June 2023, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) released updated endorsement guidelines to support the growing practice of influencer marketing. As platforms and content have evolved, the agency has continued to review practices and has issued updated guidance to ensure consumers are appropriately informed when influencer partnerships exist. 

In this episode of 'The fyi by Find Your Influence', host Jamie Reardon Evans, CEO/Cofounder of Find Your Influence and moderator Raro Lae Abugo, Senior Account Manager at Find Your Influence, Media Personality and Event host are joined by The Federal Trade Commission Lead Attorney, Michael Ostheimer. We discuss the recent Federal Trade Commissions updated endorsement guidelines, meant to support the growing practice of influencer marketing. 

In this productive conversation we dissect what the latest FTC guidelines updates mean,  what changes are relevant to Influencers, Agencies and Brands alike, and where to download these resources and guides to assist in ensuring all involved in the Influencer Marketing space are compliant. 

Don't miss future 'Fyi by Find Your Influence' online events. You can access past and future events through: 

Website: https://findyourinfluence.com/the-fyi-by-find-your-influence/ 

Join Our Community - to have real-time conversations with all stakeholders within the Influencer Marketing Industry: 

Facebook Group: https://www.facebook.com/groups/thefyibyfindyourinfluence 
LinkedIn Group: https://www.linkedin.com/groups/14266131/ 

Check Out FYI's Social Media: 
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/findyourinfluence/ 
Twitter: https://twitter.com/FindInfluence 
Pinterest: https://www.pinterest.com/findyourinfluence/ 
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/FindYourInfluence 

FTC Guideline Resources:
- FTC Endorsement Guides: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/ftcs-endorsement-guides-what-people-are-asking
- Disclosures 101 For Social Media Influencers: https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/documents/plain-language/1001a-influencer-guide-508_1.pdf
- Guides Concerning Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-255
-FTC Email Address for Compliance Questions:  endorsements@ftc.gov 

Follow Jamie Reardon Evans:
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jamiereardon/

Follow Raro Lae: 
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/RaroLae/ 
Podcast: https://www.youtube.com/@therldjshow Raro Lae and Davy J Show

metadata.title: FTC Reminds Influencers/Brands to Disclose  - Mini Law Lesson
metadata.author: Brian Heidelberger
metadata.shortDescription:
After reviewing numerous Instagram posts by celebrities, athletes, and other influencers, Federal Trade Commission staff recently sent out more than 90 letters reminding influencers and marketers that influencers should clearly and conspicuously disclose their relationships to brands when promoting or endorsing products through social media.

Attorney Brian Heidelberger gives you the details

know that they send out 90 letters to both celebrities athletes and other influencers as well as brands reminding everyone to clearly and conspicuously disclose the material connection when there is a relationship and they are posting on social media now this was in response to a petition filed by a company or an organization called Public Citizen as well as or other organizations who were seeing many influencer posts that were not disclosing relationship now the FTC reminded us that a material connection should be clearly and conspicuously disclosed and that's when you've got a business or family relationship a monetary payment or you received a free gift of the product and you're posting about it on social media now specifically both the public citizen complaint as well as the FTC letters addressed Instagram post as we know Instagram is becoming a hot forum for not only major celebrities and athletes but also those lower-end influencers which are seeing a lot of traction these days and the FTC reminded not only do you need to clearly and conspicuously disclose but they explain that that disclosure needs to be prominent and it cannot be past the click to receive more button and the reason for that is the FTC wants people to see the disclosure right away not have to click to see more information because frankly many people don't do that so what has the FTC also told us well they said that disclosure of the connection in a group of hashtags is no good people aren't going to see understand notice that so you want to separate out your disclosure of material connection from a group of long and other hashtags the FTC also pointed out that disclosures like hashtag SP hashtag like thanks brand or hashtag partner may not be specific enough disclosure such that people understand there is a connection now that raised a lot of questions with clients this week of hey we disclosed we have partnered with XYZ company isn't that good enough disclosure and I think that it's possible that it may be the FTC hasn't necessarily singled out the word partner such that it can never be used and it's not appropriate ever what they've indicated is hashtag partner alone especially in a clump of other hashtags isn't enough disclosure it may be and I'm not entirely clear at this point that something like I've partnered with hashtag brand would be sufficient so what else have we learned from the FTC well in their letter to brands the FTC has noted that if brands have a specific social media policy it should address how it handles influencers and the FTC indicated that you brands if you don't have a policy that addresses how you handles influencers specifically you should really consider coming up with one so what should be in that influencer policy well we've created a number of them for clients and we hope to have a couple very easy to understand bullet points first agree in advance what the influencer is going to say as a disclosure it's not probably enough to say comply with FTC requirements or disclose your connection you really want to tell them what to say or get an agreement as to what they're going to say otherwise they might use their own judgment they might do the wrong thing and you ultimately might be liable so what should they disclose well of course hashtag a door advertisement is great and it's especially necessary if you were involved in the creation of the content the FTC has said previously before the things like hashtag sponsors sponsored are only appropriate in those situations where you really didn't have input into the content and people are giving their impartial opinion so you can do that creatively of course organically by saying I partnered with this brand to create this content or even shorter the brand and I created this content together that would get to the fact that you had input as the brand or the agency into the content now what other bullet points do you want well the disclosure needs to be at the top of the post it should be separated it out and it should be in a font and style easily read and understood it should be if for a video both in the video itself and we would advise in the description although I don't think the FTC has specifically said that disclosure in a bio of an influencer isn't isn't good enough and of course you want the disclosure in each post and people shouldn't have to scroll down or as we just learned from the FTC click a more button to see the disclosure for live streaming video you want the disclosure and multiple points along the video because people jump in in and out and of course as the agency or advertiser you want to make sure that your deal with the influencer says that if they fail to disclose that you can get them to change their post or to take it down and if they continue to fail that you have the right to terminate your relationship with them and maybe even get a refund now these things these rules don't apply if there is no endorsement or product claims made if this is mere product placement then the disclosure rules probably aren't necessary and the FTC has told us that before so we hope this information is helpful and you start putting together your influencer guidelines if you don't have them if you want more information on mini law lessons you can go to youtube.com backslash Brian heidelberger and until next time let's be careful out there

Venable partners Len Gordon and Alexandra Megaris will present “What You Need to Know About FTC’s Proposed Changes to Its Endorsement Guides.” The Endorsement Guides, first issued in 1980 and last amended in 2009, reflect the Commission’s interpretation of how the FTC Act applies to endorsements and testimonials in advertising. This webinar will cover how the FTC’s proposals could impact social media marketing and use of customer reviews.

Speakers
Len Gordon, Partner, Venable LLP
Alexandra Megaris, Partner, Venable LLP

#googleads #competitorads  

Thinking of targeting your competitors in Google Ads? It can boost visibility—but it’s risky business if you don’t know the rules. In this video, Sammy Cisek breaks down when and how you can use competitor names in your ad campaigns without getting slapped with a policy violation.

=== WHAT YOU'LL LEARN ===
✅ Whether bidding on competitor keywords is allowed in Google Ads
✅ When you can (and can’t) use competitor names in your ad copy
✅ Recent changes to Google’s trademark policy you need to know
✅ Strategic tips to run competitor campaigns without wasting budget
✅ What to do if someone is bidding on your brand name

=== PREREQUISITES ===
Before testing competitor campaigns, you should:
✔️ Understand the basics of Google Ads campaign structure
✔️ Be familiar with trademark and ad copy policies
✔️ Know how to monitor brand terms and performance metrics

=== TIMESTAMPS ===
 0:00 – Intro
 0:08 – Bidding on Competitor Keywords
 0:43 – Using Competitor Names in Ad Copy
 1:48 – How to Run a Competitor Campaign Safely
 2:18 – Tips to Avoid Policy Violations
 2:40 – What to Do if Competitors Bid on You

=== TROUBLESHOOTING TIPS ===
 ❌ Ads disapproved after mentioning a competitor?
 ✔️ Check if the competitor has filed a trademark complaint.

❌ Not seeing results from your competitor campaign?
 ✔️ Try creating a separate campaign with a unique landing page and more relevant ad copy.

❌ Accidentally included competitor names via automation?
 ✔️ Turn off dynamic keyword insertion (DKI) and automatically created assets in your campaigns.

metadata.title: The Truth About Google's New Target Bidding "Update" [Inside Google Ads Episode 130]
metadata.author: Jyll Saskin Gales | Google Ads Coach
metadata.shortDescription:
Google announced a change to how budget-limited campaigns on target-based bid strategies will work... is it time to freak out? Hardly! In episode 130 of the Inside Google Ads podcast, host Jyll Saskin Gales cuts through the hyperbole to tell you what's changing, what you need to know, and what it ACTUALLY means for your campaigns. While social media is filled with "hot takes," the reality of this update is much more straightforward than the rumors suggest.

Key Topics Discussed:
- What the August 17, 2026 smart bidding update actually changes for target CPA and target ROAS campaigns
- The difference between the red "limited by budget" warning and the yellow recommendation
- Why some advertisers see an anecdotal performance "overshoot" in budget-limited campaigns
- Practical solutions for accounts that are chronically limited by budget
- How to use maximize bid strategies as an alternative to target-based bidding

You can get Inside Google Ads episodes delivered to your inbox each week by signing up for free at https://free.jyll.ca/?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=episode130

Inside Google Ads course
Join 400+ marketers like you who are mastering Google Ads with Jyll's Inside Google Ads membership course. You'll get exclusive access to JyllBot, and you can meet top industry experts at an exclusive live video call every single month. segments.text: Google Ads practitioners are all
freaking out about this new update, but
you don't have to. There's a small
change coming to smart bidding, and as
someone who is currently writing the
book all about bid strategies, I didn't
even feel the need to comment on this at
first because in my opinion, it is such
an insignificant change. However, over
the last couple of weeks, I have seen so
many friends and colleagues and not
friends commenting about this, so I
thought I would be doing you a
disservice if I didn't share with you
what's happening to target bid
strategies that are limited by budget.
In this episode, I'm going to cover what
the change actually is and why you don't
need to freak out about it and what you
should do instead. I'm your host, Jill
Saskin Gales. I spent 6 years working
for big brands at Google, and now I work
for you. This is Inside Google Ads
episode 130, target bidding change.
First things first, what's happening
here? This affects campaigns that are
limited by budget, and by that I mean
the actual red limited by budget
warning, not the yellow limited by
budget recommendation.
And it only applies to campaigns that
use target CPA or target ROAS bidding,
which from here on out I'm just going to
call target bid strategies. And the big
change is, are you ready? For campaigns
that are limited by budget, as of August
17th, 2026, your smart bidding strategy
will try to stay close to its target.
Really, that's the change. So, let's say
you have a search campaign that is
limited by budget and your target CPA is
$10, going forward, it's going to try
harder to hit a target CPA of $10. So,
why is everyone freaking out about this?
Well, some things that people had
noticed anecdotally were if you had a
campaign that was limited by budget and
you were using a target-based bid
strategy, that the smart bidding may try
to overshoot and be more efficient than
your target. So, in our example of a
search campaign with a target CPA of
$10, maybe if it was limited by budget,
it was actually hitting a real CPA
closer to $5. Again, this is not
something that was guaranteed, not
something documented, not even something
that I would observe would always
happen. Sometimes I see campaigns
overshooting their target, meaning they
have a more efficient performance, a
lower CPA than the target, or a higher
ROAS than the target. But, just as often
in other scenarios for campaigns that
are limited by budget, I see them
struggling to hit their target, meaning
the actual CPA is higher than the target
CPA, or the actual ROAS is lower than
the target ROAS. Going forward, Google
says that your target bid strategy will
now try harder to stay close to that
target. So, people are freaking out
about this as they like to do because
they like to get attention on social
media. No, no, no. If I'm doing my most
charitable interpretation, which I like
to do of Google's actions, so I will
also do of others' actions, people think
that this is Google being greedy or
selfish, or making you unnecessarily get
worse performance than you would have
otherwise. And personally, I just don't
think that's the right way to look at
this at all. Remember, your bid strategy
is how you tell Google Ads what you want
it to do. So, if you're telling Google
that you want a target CPA of $10, it
should be trying to get you $10. If your
target is $10 and it's been achieving
five, then change your target to five.
Like, what what's the big issue here?
And again, as part of that, target-based
bid strategies are not designed to be
limited by budget. I've spoken on this
podcast before about how being limited
by budget actually hinders performance.
So, if you only have a set budget to
spend, and you can't increase it, you
should either stick to a maximize bid
strategy like maximize conversions or

In this episode of the Inside Hustler's Brain Podcast, Jitendra Vasani sits down with Niels Zee at the Chiang Mai SEO Conference to discuss the future of affiliate marketing. After seeing major websites wiped out by Google’s Helpful Content Update, Niels successfully pivoted from traditional SEO to a highly profitable Google Ads strategy.
Niels reveals how he turned a 95% traffic loss into a business generating $92,000 in monthly profit by bidding on high-intent keywords rather than relying on organic rankings. As a partner in Matt Diggity’s agency, Affram, Niels breaks down the exact "conversion-first" framework that separates successful paid campaigns from failed SEO articles.
Beyond the technical strategies, the conversation dives deep into the mindset of a high-level entrepreneur. Niels shares his personal philosophy on managing stress, the importance of "frequencies" in business relationships, and why meditation and gratitude are non-negotiable for sustainable success.

Key Takeaways in This Episode:
The Pivot: Why Niels stopped relying on SEO after losing 95% of traffic and switched to Paid Ads.
The $92k Blueprint: A breakdown of the numbers: $12k revenue vs. $92k profit models.
Landing Page Masterclass: Why you must skip the "informational intro" and go straight to the "Best Product" list for ads.
CRO Tactics: How to use "Today’s Date" plugins and specific CTA designs to boost conversions by 10-15%.
The Matt Diggity Partnership: How Niels leveraged authority and data to partner with the biggest name in SEO.
Mindset & Philosophy: Handling entrepreneurial burnout, the power of gratitude, and overcoming "scarcity mindset" financial goals.

metadata.author: Paul Rooney
metadata.shortDescription:
Want a free audit of your Google Ads account? Book a call here: https://www.roonii.com/contact-us

In this video, I look at whether you should be bidding on your own brand name in Google Ads — or whether you’re just paying for clicks you’d get for free anyway.

Why the answer isn’t the same for every brand: when Edmunds and eBay both tested pausing their brand campaigns, the results were wildly different Edmunds lost around 50% of its brand ad traffic, while eBay lost just 0.5%. Same decision, two completely different outcomes.

I cover why that gap exists, the three questions to actually ask before you touch your brand campaigns:

1. Whether competitors are bidding on your brand name.

2. How much of that traffic your organic listing would capture on its own.

3. Whether your brand campaigns are generating incremental conversions or just taking credit for demand that already existed

And why the right move is to test and measure your own account rather than copy what worked (or didn’t) for someone else’s.

Our website: https://www.roonii.com/
My LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/paul-rooney-301763127/

metadata.title: How to Monetize Subscribers in the First 7 Days
metadata.author: Local Media HQ
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to grow a local newsletter without waiting months to recoup ad spend? Louis Nicholls, co-founder of SparkLoop, breaks down “zero-day payback” tactics—mixing paid recommendations, trip-wire offers, and high-value local lead-gen deals—to help operators turn every 50-cent subscriber into immediate profit.

Louis shares real-world tests (including his own) that combine three monetization layers on the thank-you page and in the first 24 hours, plus tips for negotiating $10-$100 per lead with home-service pros, gyms, and even med-spas. He also explains why sending two welcome emails the first day actually boosts engagement and weeds out the wrong readers. 

Key takeaways: focus on arbitrage cheap Facebook leads, create irresistible “free money” offers, and don’t fear higher send frequency.
Connect with Louis: growmynewsletter.com (newsletter, YouTube & resources) • Twitter/X @louisnicholls • Explore SparkLoop at sparkloop.app

#Newsletters #EmailMarketing #LocalMedia #SparkLoop #LeadGeneration #Monetization #LouisNicholls #MediaBusiness #SubscriberGrowth #DigitalPublishing

metadata.title: $1M with 1,000 Subscribers, Acquisition, Free Traffic is OVER | Louis Nicholls, SparkLoop Co-Founder
metadata.author: George Helgesen
metadata.shortDescription:
Newsletter growth is getting expensive — free traffic from Google and social is drying up, and publishers are now paying for every subscriber. Louis Nicholls, co-founder of SparkLoop, the recommendation network behind some of the biggest newsletters on the internet, breaks down what actually works now: what a subscriber costs, how publishers buy one from Meta for $2 and earn it back the same day, and whether a LinkedIn newsletter is worth keeping.

James Clear was one of SparkLoop's first 50 customers. SparkLoop was acquired by ConvertKit, now Kit, in 2023.

Also in this episode:

- Why breaking past 1M+ subscribers is a completely different game than getting to 1M
- The reason SparkLoop only lets in the top 1% of newsletters — and what that flywheel actually does
- The blank-slate moment: why the same offer converts at 2-3% in one place and 40-50% in another
- How 1,000 subscribers turned into $1M in revenue 

If you run a newsletter, own an audience you're trying to turn into a business, or spend money on paid acquisition and wonder where it actually goes — this episode is for you.

0:00 Intro  
2:06 What Is SparkLoop?  
3:20 How SparkLoop Started  
5:21 James Clear and the First Customers  
6:19 Why Big Newsletters Struggle to Grow  
7:37 From Referrals to Paid Recommendations  
11:52 How SparkLoop Matches Newsletters  
15:44 What Does a Subscriber Cost?  
17:16 The Kit Acquisition  
22:18 Should I Move My Newsletter Off LinkedIn?  
28:11 The End of Free Traffic  
30:45 How Publishers Arbitrage Meta Ads  
33:36 Why SparkLoop Won't Build Everything  
37:01 New Tab Moments and 40-50% Opt-Ins  
40:03 Louis's Advice: Start a Newsletter

If you enjoyed this episode, please like and subscribe, share it with your network, and leave a comment.

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/georgehelgesen/  
Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/show/5a7OB49RrVoUp7I5965kWc  
Youtube: https://www.youtube.com/@georgehelgesen

👉 Follow Louis:

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/louisnicholls/  
X: https://x.com/louisnicholls_  
SparkLoop: https://sparkloop.app  
Email: louis@sparkloop.app

metadata.title: Explode Newsletter Growth with a Partner Program - newsletter growth masterclass
metadata.author: SparkLoop
metadata.shortDescription:
Can acquiring engaged, high-quality newsletter subscribers really be this easy?
 
Scaling paid newsletter growth is incredibly hard. But it doesn't have to be...

Imagine you could create a system where:

→ hundreds of top newsletters and influencers in your niche recommend your newsletter
→ you automatically screen and assess the subscribers they send your way — to make sure they're high-quality and engaged with your newsletter
→ you pay a fixed price — only for valuable subscribers

You can. It's called a partner program. And hundreds of top newsletters and publishers — like Front Office Sports, 1440 and the Daily Upside — are using it to drive unbeatable newsletter growth. 

The results are almost unbelievable:

→ acquire up to 100k new, high-quality subscribers/month
→ pay a fixed price per "valuable" subscriber — with a fixed budget
→ only a 60min setup and zero ongoing work

And you can join them!

In this masterclass, Louis — our cofounder at SparkLoop — shows you the blueprint for how to set up a partner program that'll drive huge amounts of high-quality subscriber growth for your newsletter. At your target acquisition cost and with minimal effort.

You'll learn...

→ how to set up an effective partner program for different kinds of newsletters. From niche B2B to local media and broad-focus publications
→ secrets from running 100+ partner programs for the world's top publishers
→ how to set your CPA, budget, and targeting to ensure you only attract high-value subscribers
... and much more!

If you have an established publication and are ready to scale your newsletter growth to the next level in 2023 then this masterclass is perfect for you.

Check it out: https://sparkloop.app/partner-program

In this episode, SparkLoop's Dylan Redekop chats with Josh Spector—marketing strategist and publisher of For The Interested: a one-paragraph newsletter for experts with simple, proven ways to use writing to grow your business.

Josh has been publishing For The Interested for 8 years and has built a substantial following transforming his insights into a pivotal resource for experts aiming to monetize their skills.

In this episode, Dylan & Josh explore:
→ Rapid Growth Techniques: How can small, daily actions significantly boost your newsletter subscriber count? Josh unveils practical, bite-sized strategies.

→ Engagement Metrics: What’s the single most telling metric for newsletter success, and how can it guide your content strategy?

→ Advertisement Innovation: Why traditional newsletter ads fail and how a simple shift in focus can multiply your click-through rates.

→ Revenue Boosting Moves: Josh discusses straightforward levers you can pull to dramatically increase your newsletter’s income.

→ A Thought-Provoking Take: Are we really in a newsletter bubble? Josh shares his unique perspective on the state of the newsletter industry.

...and much more

Enjoying the podcast? Then you'll LOVE the Send & Grow newsletter where we share deep dives, tips, and news for smart newsletter operators like you.

===================================================

In this episode, SparkLoop's Dylan Redekop chats with Geoff Sharpe of Lookout Media, a pioneer in the burgeoning sphere of local newsletters.

Lookout Media, with its distinctive newsletters like Vancity Lookout and Ottawa Lookout, is revolutionizing local news by delivering stories that matter directly to your inbox. 

In this episode, Dylan & Geoff discuss…

→ The Genesis of Lookout Media: how Geoff identified a niche for local newsletters in Canada's media landscape

→ Keys to Local Newsletter Success: the essential elements that have fueled Lookout Media's growth and how they differentiate themselves from other local media

→ Innovative Growth Strategies: learn how Lookout Media expands its reader base in competitive cities.

→ Monetization Mastery: Geoff shares Lookout Media's unique formula for reliable & diversified revenue.

→ Expanding the Scope: why they've branched into food journalism and how diversification has enriched their offerings and audience engagement

→ Valuable Advice for Operators: Geoff offers tips for local media operators based on his experiences, successes, and failures.

...and much more

metadata.title: $350k with a local newsletter business — with Ryan Sneddon of Naptown Scoop
metadata.author: SparkLoop
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, SparkLoop's Dylan Redekop chats with Ryan Sneddon of Naptown Scoop, a pioneering local newsletter dedicated to Annapolis, Maryland.

In less than four years, Ryan's grown Naptown Scoop to a full-fledged local media business with a small staff and a target annual revenue of $350k. He plans to grow to over $1M in revenue in the upcoming few years—all from a local newsletter with under 18k subscribers. 

In this episode, Dylan & Ryan explore:
→ The Genesis of Naptown Scoop: How Ryan's dissatisfaction with traditional employment pathways led him to create a local newsletter that now connects thousands.

→ Overcoming Growth Challenges: Strategies and insights on expanding a local newsletter's reach and engagement, including the pivotal role of community involvement.

→ Monetization Pathways: From direct advertising to innovative community events, Ryan shares how Naptown Scoop has turned local attention into a thriving business model.

→ The Power of Local Influence: How owning a local newsletter opens unparalleled opportunities for business ventures, partnerships, and community impact.

→ Future Visions: Ryan's ambitious plans for Naptown Scoop and advice for aspiring newsletter creators looking to make a difference in their communities.

...and much more, including Ryan's candid thoughts on the balance between being a local 'celebrity' and a committed newsletter operator.

metadata.title: Free Newsletter Masterclass: Turn New Readers into Revenue
metadata.author: SparkLoop
metadata.shortDescription:
There's a 30-second window in your newsletter that matters more than almost anything else you do...

... the moment right after someone hits subscribe.

As Matt Paulson, founder of Marketbeat, puts it, "your readers will never be as engaged again as they are right after subscribing".

It's the perfect opportunity to delight your new readers, earn meaningful revenue, and unlock valuable data about who that reader is (and if they were worth spending money to acquire).

But most newsletters totally waste the opportunity — with a bad welcome survey or (worse) just a plain old "thanks for subscribing page".

Not you. Not anymore.

For the last 18 months, Louis and the SparkLoop team have helped the world's top newsletters turn that "post signup" moment into the highest-performing sign-up flows that exist.

And this Thursday, we're running a free masterclass to show you how to do it for yours.

You'll learn how to:

1. Build a sign-up flow that earns back 100%+ of what it costs to acquire a subscriber — so you can scale with high-quality subscribers from Meta ads and other paid channels, essentially for free.
2. Run a welcome survey that most of your subscribers actually complete, telling you what you genuinely need to know about them.
3. Use your sign-up flow to surface dream sponsors already hiding in plain sight.
4. Turn new subscribers into buyers for your products and services.
5. Drive higher engagement on your welcome email — and every email after it.

We'll walk through real examples of how the best newsletters are already doing this, including their actual numbers.

It's built for everyone from total beginners to large media brands, in every niche — local, consumer news, finance, B2B, and beyond.

And everything we cover, you can implement completely free in under 60 minutes.

Honestly, there isn't a single other thing you could do for your newsletter this year with anywhere near this much impact.

metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, SparkLoop's Dylan Redekop sits down with Alex Brogan of Faster Than Normal.

Faster Than Normal began as a curiosity-fuelled project but has quickly evolved into a vital resource for over 70k+ subscribers who are learning insightful mental models, concepts, and frameworks for personal growth.

In this episode, Dylan and Alex discuss...

→ The Genesis of Faster Than Normal: How Alex's journey from an early passion project to a substantial newsletter unfolded.

→ Strategic Growth Tactics: The pivotal role of social media, LinkedIn's fertile ground, and leveraging platforms like SparkLoop and Refind for exponential subscriber growth.

→ The Pitfalls and Peaks: Lessons learned from experiments in growth strategies, including the underestimated power of paid and organic recommendations.

→ Monetization Insights: From sponsored content to affiliate marketing, discover the strategies that turned Faster Than Normal into a profitable media venture.

→ The Infinite Game: Alex shares his long-term vision for the newsletter, focusing on providing unmatched value to entrepreneurs and business leaders.

→ ...and so much more!

metadata.title: How two friends joined forces to scale their newsletter — with Tyler Parker & Colton Sakamoto
metadata.author: SparkLoop
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of SparkLoop's Send & Grow podcast, Dylan Redekop chats with Tyler Parker & Colton Sakamoto, the co-founders of Office Party, a free 2x-weekly newsletter that's a curated guide for career advancement, tackling everything from job market trends to the impact of AI on employment.

Colton and Tyler's partnership approach in managing and growing Office Party is a path far less traveled in the newsletter space—which is what makes this conversation unique and fascinating. 

In this episode, Dylan, Colton, and Tyler discuss...
→ How they decided to split up their roles and why.
→ Their collaborative approach to growing the subscriber base—with a surprising & successful Facebook strategy.
→Their insights on the benefits, challenges, and dynamics of running a  newsletter as a duo.
→ Whether or not you should consider a partner for your newsletter

...and much more!

metadata.title: How to Increase Newsletter Conversions From 7% to 35% | Marketing Max | Send & Grow 2.0 Ep. 7
metadata.author: SparkLoop
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you turn a newsletter into a thriving media business? 📈

In this episode of Send and Grow, Hunter Kallay sits down with Max, better known as Marketing Max, to unpack how he went from working on Wall Street to building a marketing agency, growing a newsletter business with hundreds of thousands of subscribers, and acquiring other newsletters.

Max shares the strategies behind his growth, including how he increased a newsletter landing page's conversion rate from around 7% to 35–40%, why your opinions can be your biggest advantage as a newsletter creator, and how to make more money from the audience you've already built.

Whether you're launching your first newsletter or looking to scale an established media business, this conversation is packed with actionable insights on growth, monetization, and building a newsletter people actually want to read.

Follow Max on X: Marketing Max  
Website: https://marketingmax.io

Send and Grow explores the people, strategies, and stories behind some of the most interesting newsletters and media businesses in the world.

Subscribe for more conversations about newsletter growth, audience building, monetization, and the future of digital media.

#NewsletterGrowth #EmailMarketing #CreatorEconomy

metadata.author: Digital Niche Agency
metadata.shortDescription:
Generative engine optimization (GEO) is how you get ChatGPT and Claude to retrieve, cite, and recommend your brand. A third of search traffic has already migrated to AI platforms, and the brands with the clearest evidence trail win the recommendation.

In this webinar, DNA CEO Jason Fishman and Head of Content Khalil Doheny walk through the complete GEO system, from prompt panel to measurement. You will leave with the exact framework DNA uses on its own marketing and its investor acquisition campaigns, including a capital raise that hit its full goal in a matter of weeks, with a six-figure investment coming from a single ad.

What you'll learn:

- The six-part GEO system: prompt panel, baseline, source map, answer-ready structure, authority engine, measurement
- How to build a revenue-weighted prompt panel across the full decision journey
- How to score prompts on value, evidence, gap, and win before creating content
- Why ChatGPT and Claude must be tested as separate environments
- The technical access test to run before rewriting any content
- Weak copy vs answer-ready copy, with real examples
- How to structure pages around complete decisions with fit and poor-fit conditions
- Why Reddit and Google reviews carry outsized weight in AI recommendations
- The monitoring approach for detecting answer drift week over week

Download the free webinar deck here: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1Ev7K5YsQ22JtSWtnAA4KeyA43wQEjALBRGpgPMpfBV0/edit?usp=sharing

metadata.title: Generative Engine Optimization: How to Build Visibility in AI Searches like ChatGPT and Perplexity
metadata.author: E-commerce Berlin Expo
metadata.shortDescription:
Watch this exclusive presentation recorded live at the E-commerce Berlin Expo 2026! Gain valuable insights and explore key discussions from industry experts that will help you stay ahead in the world of e-commerce.

Speakers: 

Paul Labetzke, Senior SEO Consultant, Claneo
Nina Sausmikat, Manager Digital Websites, Henkel

Connect: 
https://www.linkedin.com/in/paul-labetzke-953a01179/
https://www.linkedin.com/in/nina-emely-sausmikat-3a55aa238/

Full title: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO): How to Build Visibility in AI Searches like ChatGPT and Perplexity

Presentation description: Google is increasingly providing direct answers. AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Perplexity are answering user questions without requiring a single click to a website. But what does this mean for brands that have relied on organic visibility for years?

Henkel faces exactly this challenge with its brands like Pattex, Loctite, and Pritt: In a world where the way people search for information is fundamentally changing, the question arises of how to stay visible. Henkel has invested heavily in SEO over the past years, generating millions of clicks annually. But what happens when those clicks start to disappear?

In this session, Nina Sausmikat (Henkel) and Paul Labetzke (Claneo) will show how companies can stay visible in the new era of AI search through Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and why the future of brand visibility needs to be reimagined now.

***

Don’t miss out on the latest trends and discussions shaping the industry. Stay updated and be part of the conversation by subscribing to our channel!

Mark your calendars for the 11th edition of the E-commerce Berlin Expo: join us for two full days of exploration, learning, and connection on February 17-18th, 2027.
