segments.text: Hello, it's me Gintarė from Trendos. In this video, I'm going to explain the term GEO,
generative engine optimization. And by the end, you will understand not what it is,
but how AI actually decides who to mention and what you can do to get in. So, let's start simple.
What is GEO? It's the practice of getting your brand mentioned and recommended inside AI answers.
The ones you get from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI overviews and Claude. To do GEO well,
you need to know where AI actually gets its information. This is the most important idea
in this whole video. So stay with me. AI has two sources and they work very differently.
The first is training data. This is the huge pile of text the model learned from originally. books,
websites, articles, transcripts, basically a snapshot of the internet. The catch is the
training data is a snapshot. It's frozen at a point in time. So if you launch last month,
the model may not know you exist yet, at least not from the training. That's where the second source
comes in, real time retrieval. When the question needs fresh or specific information, the engine
goes out and searches the web, pulls back a set of pages, reads them, and writes an answer based on
what it found. Same idea as a search engine, just feeding on AI instead of results page. So now,
why does this matter for you? It means there are two ways to get into AI answers. One, be mentioned
so constantly across the web that you're part of what the model already knows. Two, make sure your
content is strong enough to get pulled in when the AI search is live. And here's the good news. That
second one is mostly SEO. Ranking well, earning mentions, publishing genuinely useful content,
those skills carries straight over. Now, here's where it gets interesting and where AI search
really breaks from Google. When you type one question, the AI doesn't search for that one
thing. It fans your questions out into a whole set of smaller questions and runs them at once. Then
it pulls from all of those and merges everything into one answer. What it means for you is huge.
You can't win by optimizing one page for one keyword anymore. You have to be genuinely useful
across a whole topic. So how does AI decide what to actually mention? And this is the part people
get wrong in normal search. If you are position three today, you're roughly position three
tomorrow. AI is not like that. It's probabilistic. Ask the same question five times and you might get
named three of those times and your competitor twice. There's no fixed slot to own. That's
exactly why we talk about AI visibility instead of AI rankings. Think of it as a probability,
not a leaderboard position. But there are clear patterns in what gets mentioned more often and
you can work with them. Consensus matters. If lots of sources say the same thing about you,
the AI is more likely to repeat it. Freshness matters. AI learns toward recent information,
especially on topics that change, and authority still matters. Pages and brands that are already
trusted in normal search have a real head start. Notice something? There are the same fundamentals
good marketers already care about. GEO doesn't replace that work. it sits on top of it. Okay,
now you understand how the machine works. So, here's the real question. How do you actually
get your brand into these answers? There are two ways, a short-term one and a long-term one. And
you want to do both. Short-term first because it's the fastest win and almost nobody does it.
Think about who's getting named instead of you. Most of the time it's your competitors showing up
more and more on the third party sources the AI trusts. Reviews, comparisons, roundups, forums,
YouTube. The AI reads those and repeats what it finds. So the short-term move is to get mentioned
on those same sources first. The catch is finding them because you can't guess which ones matter
most. That's why we build citations by domain for. Let me show you real data. This is your own
Trendos view for the running shoes question across all engines. Look at the top sited domains. Number

metadata.title: Generative Engine Optimization: The 5-Part GEO Playbook
metadata.author: Da Hoang
metadata.shortDescription:
Generative engine optimization (GEO) is how a brand gets named inside an AI answer, not just ranked in ten blue links. Here is the full playbook, taken apart from one 52-week master plan.

We follow a sample SEO + AIO plan for a luxury sedan launch, the Lumina V8, run by one SEO lead and a stack of AI tools across North America, Europe and the Middle East. You'll see how it maps buyer prompts, builds pages made to rank in Google AI Overviews, makes them machine-readable with JSON-LD, earns tier-one mentions through digital PR, and measures share of AI voice instead of traffic.

Key points
• Buyers ask full questions, not two-word keywords: the plan opens with a matrix of 100 questions tagged by market and intent
• Each of 20 pillar pages opens with "snippet bait": a straight answer under 50 words, real numbers, no hype
• AI drafts outlines, translations and table code; people write the physical experience, under a real, named author (target: over 80% human-written)
• JSON-LD (Car + Product) gives the machine engine, price and availability; hreflang links each market's folder
• Speed is part of the luxury: main content in under 1.5 s, zero layout shift
• Digital PR instead of bought links: a data report, "The Sound of Silence", pitched to 50 journalists
• The new scoreboard: share of AI voice across 50 money keywords (target over 60%, alert below 40%)
• Guardrail: a next step (configure the car, book a test drive) right under the snippet, in case citations shrink

Chapters
0:00 Generative engine optimization: the new game
0:39 Part 1: Prompts, not keywords
1:12 Part 2: Answer first, built for Google AI Overviews
1:56 Part 3: Make it machine-readable (JSON-LD, hreflang)
2:25 Part 4: Earn the mentions with digital PR
3:07 Part 5: Share of AI voice, the new scoreboard
3:45 Takeaway: how to get cited in AI answers

The Lumina V8 is the example brand in the plan; all figures are the plan's targets, not results.
Narration: AI-generated voice.

#GenerativeEngineOptimization #GEO #AIOverviews #SEO #DigitalMarketing #DigitalPR

how to rank website in ai overview

segments.text: A buyer types one question into ChatGPT.
Which executive sedan is the quietest in the back seat, at high speed?
The AI writes one answer.
Your brand is in it, or it isn't.
That's the new game: generative engine optimization, or GEO. Getting AI to
cite you.
Here is one master plan. 52 weeks, one luxury sedan: the Lumina V8.
Run by one SEO lead and a stack of AI tools.
And traffic isn't its top metric.
The plan has five parts.
Prompts. Answers. Data. Mentions. And a new scoreboard.
Each part earns the brand a place in that answer.
Part one: prompts, not keywords.
Wealthy buyers no longer type "luxury car".
They ask full questions, about real experience, running costs, and rivals.
So the plan opens with a matrix of 100 questions.
Each one is tagged by market, and by intent.
How does it compare to a Bentley Flying Spur, for rear-seat noise?
What will it cost me over 5 years in the UAE?
Those questions feed 20 pillar pages, each at the centre of a topic cluster.
So what does a page that AI wants to quote look like?
Part two: answer first.
At the top of the page sits the snippet bait.
Under 50 words. A straight answer, with real numbers, and no hype.
Below it, a data table: power, top speed, cabin noise.
Then human proof: a quote from the technical director, and a test-drive video.
Then real maintenance costs, and five FAQs marked up as schema.
AI drafts the outline, the translations, and the table code.
People write what AI can't feel.
The Nappa leather on the wheel. The suspension over a speed bump.
Every article has a real author, with a real LinkedIn profile.
After editing, the target is over 80% human-written.
People can read that page. Can a machine?
Part three: make it machine-readable.
Every product page carries a block of JSON-LD.
It tells the machine: this is a car, and a product.
A 4.0-litre V8 hybrid. $150,000. In stock.
One domain, a folder for each market, all cross-linked with hreflang tags.
And speed is part of the luxury.
Main content in under 1.5 seconds. Zero layout shift.
The site is readable now. But why would AI trust it?
Part four: earn the mentions.
Trust comes from what others say about you.
So, no bought guest posts, and no forum links.
Instead: digital PR.
The target list: 50 journalists, at titles like Top Gear, Car and Driver, and
AutoBild.
The pitch is a data story.
"The Sound of Silence": cabin decibel data from 100 cars, over 10 years.
Its aim: prove this cabin is the quietest on record.
A report like that is built to earn links on its own.
AI reads each journalist's recent work, and drafts the pitch.
But the moment a journalist replies, a person takes over.
So how do you know any of it is working?
Part five: the new scoreboard.
Remember the metric that isn't traffic?
It's share of AI voice.
Across 50 money keywords, how often does AI name your brand?
The target is over 60%. Below 40%, an alert fires.
Beside it: 20 tier-one press mentions a month.
The finish line, by December: a top-three AI citation in the US and Germany.
And 1,500 test-drive or quote requests.
One risk remains: Google can shrink the citation box, and clicks drop.
So right under the snippet sits a next step.
Configure the car. Book a test drive.
So here's the shift. In AI search, you don't rank for a keyword.
You get cited in an answer.
Map the questions. Answer first. Make it machine-readable. Earn the mentions.
Track your share of AI voice.
Start with one buyer question, and write its 50-word answer.

That's the new game: generative engine optimization, or GEO. Getting AI to cite you. Here is one master plan. 52 weeks, one luxury sedan: the Lumina V8. Run by one SEO lead and a stack of AI tools. And traffic isn't its top metric. The plan has five parts. Prompts. Answers. Data. Mentions. And a new scoreboard. Each part earns the brand a place in that answer. Part one: prompts, not keywords. Wealthy buyers no longer type "luxury car". They ask full questions, about real experience, running costs, and rivals. So the plan opens with a matrix of 100 questions. Each one is tagged by market, and by intent. How does it compare to a Bentley Flying Spur, for rear-seat noise? What will it cost me over 5 years in the UAE? Those questions feed 20 pillar pages, each at the centre of a topic cluster. So what does a page that AI wants to quote look like? Part two: answer first. At the top of the page sits the snippet bait. Under 50 words. A straight answer, with real numbers, and no hype. Below it, a data table: power, top speed, cabin noise. Then human proof: a quote from the technical director, and a test-drive video. Then real maintenance costs, and five FAQs marked up as schema. AI drafts the outline, the translations, and the table code. People write what AI can't feel. The Nappa leather on the wheel. The suspension over a speed bump. Every article has a real author, with a real LinkedIn profile. After editing, the target is over 80% human-written. People can read that page. Can a machine? Part three: make it machine-readable. Every product page carries a block of JSON-LD. It tells the machine: this is a car, and a product. A 4.0-litre V8 hybrid. $150,000. In stock. One domain, a folder for each market, all cross-linked with hreflang tags. And speed is part of the luxury. Main content in under 1.5 seconds. Zero layout shift. The site is readable now. But why would AI trust it? Part four: earn the mentions. Trust comes from what others say about you. So, no bought guest posts, and no forum links. Instead: digital PR. The target list: 50 journalists, at titles like Top Gear, Car and Driver, and AutoBild. The pitch is a data story. "The Sound of Silence": cabin decibel data from 100 cars, over 10 years. Its aim: prove this cabin is the quietest on record. A report like that is built to earn links on its own. AI reads each journalist's recent work, and drafts the pitch. But the moment a journalist replies, a person takes over. So how do you know any of it is working? Part five: the new scoreboard. Remember the metric that isn't traffic? It's share of AI voice. Across 50 money keywords, how often does AI name your brand? The target is over 60%. Below 40%, an alert fires. Beside it: 20 tier-one press mentions a month. The finish line, by December: a top-three AI citation in the US and Germany. And 1,500 test-drive or quote requests. One risk remains: Google can shrink the citation box, and clicks drop. So right under the snippet sits a next step. Configure the car. Book a test drive. So here's the shift. In AI search, you don't rank for a keyword. You get cited in an answer. Map the questions. Answer first. Make it machine-readable. Earn the mentions. Track your share of AI voice. Start with one buyer question, and write its 50-word answer.
